facts.statement: The study found that extracellular vesicles from both human and non-human cells all slowed down the formation of amyloid-beta fibrils at similar rates.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: When researchers used enzymes to strip surface proteins off the vesicles, the vesicles became much better at stopping amyloid-beta aggregation.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: Removing the sugar chains (glycans) attached to surface proteins also changed the vesicles' ability to inhibit aggregation, but the effect was much smaller than removing the proteins themselves.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: The authors suggest that lipids are the main drivers of the inhibition, while surface proteins act like a switch to tune how strong that inhibition is.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: Taking off proteoglycans (a type of sugar-protein complex) caused a small but reliable increase in the vesicles' ability to stop aggregation.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: The results imply that slowing down amyloid-beta clumping is a shared characteristic of extracellular vesicles from many different cell types.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue
